newsitem.title: INDIA: India edible oil trade says worried by low output.
newsitem.headline: India edible oil trade says worried by low output.

text.p: India's edible oil trade on Sunday expressed concern over a growing gap between domestic supply and demand, and called on the government to take urgent steps to increase oilseeds productivity.

"The widening gap between demand and supply in recent years necessitates a thorough review of the government's strategy," Central Organisation of Oil Industry and Trade (COOIT) president Dhanji Sawla told a seminar on India's summer oilseeds crop.
Most recent increases in oilseeds output arose from the expansion of area under cultivation, Sawla said.
"It is now evident that further incremental growth in oilseeds production would have to increasingly depend upon higher productivity per hectare," he said.

India's oilseeds production swelled to around 22 million tonnes in 1993/94 (November-October) from 11.68 million tonnes in 1986/87 as the cultivation area grew to 26 million hectares (64 million acres) from 19 million hectares (47 million acres).
Since then, output has been stagnant.
COOIT officials on Saturday said India would need to import between 1.4 and 1.5 million tonnes of edible oil in 1996/97 against 1.14 million tonnes in 1995/96.
Sawla said India's per-hectare oilseeds yield was around 850 kg per hectare -- barely one-third of the world's best yield.
"The progress of several key factors like irrigation, high-yielding, pest-resistant and drought varieties and timely supply of inputs has left much room for improvement," Sawla said.
He said the government would need to undertake extensive research and development to augment productivity.

Industry officials also urged the government to permit India to import oilseeds, which would help activate idle crushing capacity, estimated at 60 percent, and earn foreign exchange through exports of extractions.

"It is a government decision (on allowing oilseeds imports) which we hope will be favourable," COOIT special adviser O.P. Goenka told Reuters. Industry officials said India had the potential to produce about 2.5 million tonnes of edible oil from non-conventional sources such as rice bran.
"With an available potential of 2.5 million tonnes of non-conventional oils, we are presently producing about 1.3 million," Sawla said.
"With our demand for edible oil continuously rising, the country can ill afford to let such vast resources remain untapped."
India is expected to produce 6.7 million tonnes of edible oil in 1996/97 compared with 6.55 million in 1995/96, a COOIT statement said.

Industry officials said both trade and the government needed to act swiftly to foster India's nascent oil palm cultivation programme. India currently produces about 5,000 tonnes of palm olein annually.
